title: Purifying, growing
hookLine: the word means both to purify and to grow

lines: A GARDENER CUTS A HEALTHY ROSE.
cards: A gardener walks out with shears and starts cutting a healthy rosebush. Whole stems, buds still on them, onto the ground. Someone watching winces: you're ruining it.
The gardener says, wait until spring. A cut in the right place, and the plant comes back fuller. Taking away is how it grows.
One of the pillars of Islam is built on a word that does the same strange thing. It's usually translated as alms, or charity, or the poor-due. But the word carries two meanings at once.

teach.h: ONE ROOT: TO BE PURE, TO GROW.
teach.b: You met zakat back on day nineteen, as the pillar about money. Today, slowly, the word itself.
First, it comes from a root, z-k-w, that the classical Arabic dictionaries give two senses for: to be pure, and to grow, to increase. Lane's Arabic-English lexicon lists both.
So zakat is, in one word, a cleaning and a growing. Second, the Qur'an uses both together.
In surah nine the Prophet ﷺ is told, in Pickthall's words: "Take alms of their wealth, wherewith thou mayst purify them and mayst make them grow." Notice who is purified. Not the money.
Them, the givers. The alms do something to the person who gives, not only to the one who receives. Third, the growing.

The Qur'an pictures spending in Allah's way as a single grain that sprouts seven ears, with a hundred grains in every ear. And a hadith in Sahih Muslim has the Prophet ﷺ say that charity does not decrease wealth.
On a calculator, that can't be right. The tradition is pointing at a different arithmetic, where what grows is blessing, and the giver.
Fourth, why it's a pillar and not just a kind thing to do. Zakat isn't a mood of generosity.

teach.h: WHEREWITH THOU MAYST PURIFY THEM AND MAYST MAKE THEM GROW.
teach.b: It's an obligation, measured and regular, with rules about who pays, how much, and to whom, and the next days walk through them one at a time. Underneath the rules sits this word.
The rules give the amount; the word gives what it's for. Not how much is lost, but what this makes room for.

how: Muslims who meet the conditions pay zakat as a set share of their wealth each year, and teachers describe it with Qur'an 9:103 as purifying the giver as well as helping the receiver.

games.q: you've just given away part of your savings. on paper, you have less. what does the hadith in Sahih Muslim say?
o: charity decreases wealth, but it's worth it.
charity only counts if no one knows.
games.why: charity does not decrease wealth. the tradition is pointing at a growth the calculator doesn't show.

practice: Choose one thing you could give, a few coins, a meal, an hour, a coat you don't wear, and breathe in, noticing whatever part of you wants to hold on.
Breathe out and picture it already given, then notice what happens in your chest and shoulders: heavier, lighter, or no change.

wordCard.voice: Zakat. A pillar of Islam: a set share of wealth given each year. From a root that means both to purify and to grow. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the pillar of giving, from a root meaning to be pure and to grow.
